 Workers’ Wage Increases in Iran Lag Far Behind Inflation
 By Sia Rajabi 
 -
 October 31, 2026 
 Share 
 Facebook X Pinterest Linkedin ReddIt 
 The wage increase at the beginning of the year (March 22, 2026) has failed to bridge the gap between income and living expenses, as a new wave of price hikes has eroded the purchasing power of working-class households. Independent labor calculations now put the cost of a basic living basket for households in the fourth income decile at 780 million rials (approximately $289). According to a workers’ representative on the Supreme Labor Council, this figure has increased by 360 million rials (approximately $133) over six months. However, no further meeting has been held to pursue a wage adjustment since the Supreme Labor Council’s last session on September 19, leaving workers’ demands for a wage review unresolved. The current minimum wage for a worker with two children is approximately $92 per month.
 Annual Inflation Hits 76.8% in Iran as Prices Rise 4.4% in October 
 Mohsen Bagheri, a member of the workers’ delegation to the Supreme Labor Council, told the state-run Khabar Online news website that the latest calculations of working-class household expenses show that the cost of a basic living basket for the fourth income decile has reached 780 million rials (approximately $289). According to calculations by the wage task force of the nationwide Association of Islamic Labor Councils, this figure represents the minimum living expenses for households in this income group.
 Emphasizing that the current minimum wage is sufficient for a household of 3.3 people for no more than nine days, Bagheri said: The current wage therefore does not even cover one-third of a household’s expenses for an entire month.
 According to Bagheri, the cost of the basic living basket has increased by 360 million rials since December, a significant rise compared with previous years. He emphasized that he could not recall the cost of the living basket increasing by such an amount over a six-month period.
 A Month Has Passed Since the Last Supreme Labor Council Meeting
 The workers’ representative on the Supreme Labor Council went on to criticize the failure to convene a new meeting of the council, saying: The last meeting was held on September 19, and no further session has taken place since then. Given the labor minister’s promise, we had expected a meeting on wage adjustments to be held shortly afterward so that this year’s wage resolution could be implemented.
 Referring to the legal requirement for monthly Supreme Labor Council meetings, Bagheri explained that meetings had been held every month through September, but no meeting took place in October. Previously, Labor Minister Ahmad Meydari had made efforts to convene the sessions, and some meetings had even taken place in his absence. However, despite requests from workers’ representatives, recent efforts to arrange another meeting have yielded no results.
 Stating that the government’s decisions will play a decisive role in advancing wage adjustments under current conditions, Bagheri added: In my view, if the government acts sooner, there is no specific obstacle to addressing wage increases, although I am unaware of any considerations within the government that might be delaying this decision.
 Inflation Could Drive Up Living Costs Further by the End of the Year
 The workers’ representative on the Supreme Labor Council also warned that rising prices could spread to non-food goods and services in the coming months, further increasing living costs.
 He said: Some of the inflationary pressure on food prices may ease, but price increases in other household expenditure categories appear likely to continue. Therefore, even if prices for some food items fall, it cannot be concluded that households’ overall cost of living has decreased.
 Delaying Wage Adjustments Will Make Year-End Decisions More Difficult
 Referring to the possibility that wage decisions could be postponed until the end of the year, Bagheri said that some might assume the issue could be settled at year-end, as in previous years, if the decision-making process were prolonged. However, such an approach carries significant risks. In that case, the government would have to account for the loss of purchasing power caused by inflation all at once when calculating year-end wages.
 Referring to the Statistical Center of Iran’s report that inflation had exceeded 73% as of September 22, Bagheri added that if inflation reaches approximately 80% by the end of the year, a substantial wage increase may be needed to compensate for the loss of purchasing power. Even such an increase would not necessarily cover the full cost of living, but it could place considerable psychological and economic pressure on the wage-setting process.
 Workers in Iran are struggling to make ends meet, and some are forced to hold multiple jobs just to cover their most basic living expenses.
